name: Huế
info: Huế is a city in central Vietnam on the Perfume River, near ruins of the 4th century CE; it was the capital of Đàng Trong under the Nguyễn lords and of all Vietnam under the Nguyễn dynasty from 1802 to 1945.

facts.founded: The oldest ruins in the area belong to the Kingdom of Lâm Ấp and date to the 4th century CE; the Nguyễn lords based themselves at Phú Xuân in 1687, and Nguyễn Ánh made it the imperial capital after 1802.
facts.where: On the Perfume River (Sông Hương) in central Vietnam, between mountains, hills, plains and a coastal lagoon, bordering Quảng Trị to the north, Đà Nẵng to the south, Laos to the west and the South China Sea to the east.
facts.known: The Cham ruins of Kandarpapura; Thuận Hóa, ceded to Đại Việt in 1306; Phú Xuân, capital of the Nguyễn lords; the capital of Vietnam under the Nguyễn dynasty, 1802 to 1945; the Imperial City and imperial tombs; the áo dài; Buddhist monasteries and Huế cuisine
facts.today: Huế is one of Vietnam's centrally governed cities, and since 2025 it has included the whole of the former Thừa Thiên Huế province.

t: The Thuận Hóa region passed from Champa to Đại Việt in 1306, and from the late 16th century the Nguyễn lords governed it and based themselves at Phú Xuân in 1687.
Phú Xuân was the capital of Đàng Trong from 1738 to 1775, fell to the Trịnh lords in 1775 and to the Tây Sơn in 1786, and was retaken in 1802 by Nguyễn Ánh, who made it the capital of all Vietnam.
It was renamed Huế in 1899 under the French, remained the seat of the Nguyễn emperors until Bảo Đại abdicated in 1945, and became a centrally governed city in 2025.
dyk: The first written use of the name Huế may be a line of a Chữ Nôm poem attributed to Emperor Lê Thánh Tông that mentions "Huế rice"; older documents called the place Phú Xuân, Kinh Đô or simply Kinh.
ev: The oldest ruins in the area, those of the Kingdom of Lâm Ấp, date from this time

sections.origins:
Huế lies in central Vietnam, and the Perfume River (Sông Hương) passes through its centre. Its territory falls into four zones: mountains, hills, plains, and lagoons separated from the sea by sandbanks. The Tam Giang–Cau Hai lagoon, the largest lagoon in Southeast Asia, is 68 kilometres long and has a surface area of 220 square kilometres, and the coastline runs for 128 kilometres.

The oldest ruins in Huế belong to the Kingdom of Lâm Ấp and date to the 4th century CE. The ruins of its capital, the ancient city of Kandarpapura, lie on Long Tho Hill, three kilometres west of the city. Kandarpapura might have been established only in the reign of Kandarpadharma (r. 629–640) and named after that king, so it may not have been the name of the capital of the earlier Lâm Ấp kingdom. Another Champa ruin nearby, the ancient city of Hoa Chau, dates to the 9th century.

The area was historically part of Thuận Hóa. In 1306 the King of Champa, Chế Mân, offered Vietnam two Cham prefectures, Ô and Lý, in exchange for marriage with a Trần princess named Huyền Trân. The Vietnamese king Trần Anh Tông accepted, and he renamed the prefectures Thuận and Hóa, which together were often called the Thuận Hóa region.
sections.growth:
The Nguyễn lords moved their seat in stages. Lord Nguyễn Hoàng (1558 to 1613) established bases at Ai Tu, Tra Bat and Dinh Cat, and the lords moved their palaces to Kim Long in 1636 before basing their operations at Phú Xuân in 1687. That year Phú Xuân also became the provincial capital, and from 1738 to 1775 it was the capital of Đàng Trong.

Dress developed there too. The áo dài, the Vietnamese national costume, developed from the clothes civilians wore in Đàng Trong in the 18th century after the costume reform of Lord Nguyễn Phúc Khoát. A court historian recorded the rules of dress in the Đại Nam thực lục, describing gowns with straight collars, seams closed on both sides and sleeves of any width. This outfit evolved into the áo ngũ thân, the five-part costume most popular in Vietnam in the 19th and 20th centuries.

After 1802 Nguyễn Ánh, later Emperor Gia Long, rebuilt the citadel entirely and made Huế the Imperial City, the capital of all Vietnam. The Imperial City, with its palaces and shrines, and the Forbidden Purple City, once reserved for the royal family, stood within a moat and stone walls. The Flag Tower and the royal tombs belong to the same period of the Nguyễn dynasty, which lasted from 1802 to 1945.
sections.rulers:
Thuận Hóa passed from Champa to Đại Việt in 1306. In 1592 the Mạc dynasty was forced to flee to Cao Bằng, and the Lê emperors were enthroned as de jure rulers under Nguyễn Kim. After Kim was poisoned and his eldest son Nguyễn Uông assassinated, Trịnh Kiểm took over the leadership. Another son, Nguyễn Hoàng, feared the same fate, pretended to be mentally ill and, through his sister Ngoc Bao, a wife of Trịnh Kiểm, obtained the governorship of Thuận Hóa, the southernmost region of Vietnam at the time. He and his heir Nguyễn Phúc Nguyên pacified it, secretly made it loyal to the Nguyễn family and then rose against the Trịnh lords, which began a civil war between the two families.

The Nguyễn lords ruled the area until the Trịnh clan conquered it in 1775. The Tây Sơn rebellion broke out in 1771, and while it fought the Nguyễn lords, the Trịnh lords sent an army south and captured Phú Xuân in 1775. Their general Hoàng Ngũ Phúc then made a tactical alliance with the Tây Sơn and withdrew almost all his troops to Tonkin. In 1786 the Tây Sơn defeated the Trịnh garrison and occupied Phú Xuân.

In 1802 Nguyễn Ánh recaptured Phú Xuân and unified the country. After the French conquest the city was renamed Huế in 1899 and remained the capital of Annam, one of the six regions of French Indochina, until the State of Vietnam was established in 1949. The emperors remained in the Imperial Palace until Bảo Đại abdicated in 1945, when the Democratic Republic of Vietnam made Hanoi its capital.
sections.life:
Among the emperors who ruled from Huế, Minh Mạng reigned from 14 February 1820 until his death on 20 January 1841. He was a younger son of Gia Long, whose eldest son, Crown Prince Cảnh, had died in 1801, and he was known for his opposition to French involvement in Vietnam and for his rigid Confucian orthodoxy.

Buddhist belief marked the life of the city. Many people in Huế keep a tradition of eating a vegetarian meal twice a month as part of their Buddhist beliefs, and all-vegetarian restaurants stand in several parts of the city. Huế dishes are known for small servings with refined presentation, a vestige of royal cuisine, and the food is often very spicy. Violet áo dài are especially common in Huế, a colour connected with the city's heritage as a former capital, and the combination of áo dài and nón lá is seen by Vietnamese as particularly evocative of the city.

The Huế Central Hospital, established in 1894, was the first Western hospital in Vietnam. In 1963 the monk Thích Quảng Đức drove from Huế to Saigon to protest the anti-Buddhist policies of the South Vietnamese government and set himself on fire on a Saigon street; photographs of the self-immolation became enduring images of the Vietnam War. The Zen master Thích Nhất Hạnh, who came from Huế, lived for years in exile, returned in October 2018 and lived at the Tu Hieu pagoda until his death in 2022.
sections.crises:
In the Tết Offensive, North Vietnamese (PAVN) and Việt Cộng forces attacked Huế in the early hours of 31 January 1968 and occupied most of the city. South Vietnamese and United States forces retook it in house-to-house fighting. The South Vietnamese flag was raised on the Citadel flag tower on 24 February, and the last operation ended on 2 March. Eighty per cent of the city was destroyed and 116,000 of its 140,000 people were made homeless. Allied dead numbered 708; PAVN-VC losses are disputed, from 1,042 in a captured PAVN document to 5,133 claimed by the American command. James Willbanks writes that 5,800 civilians were reported killed or missing, and Mark Bowden estimates more than 8,000.

During the occupation the Việt Cộng and PAVN rounded up officials, soldiers, teachers, religious leaders and foreigners from prepared lists, and many were killed. Mass graves were found in and around Huế in the following months and years. Douglas Pike's study for the United States mission estimated 2,800 victims; estimates run to almost 6,000, and South Vietnam published a list of 4,062 victims murdered or abducted. Bùi Tín later acknowledged executions of civilians, which he attributed to a breakdown of discipline under bombardment and to commanders shooting prisoners during the retreat. Ngo Vinh Long put the number at 710, Len Ackland at 300 to 400, and David Hunt called Pike's study propaganda. Mark Bowden estimates 2,000 executed, and between 200 and 2,000 civilians were killed in South Vietnamese reprisals after the battle.

After the fall of Saigon in 1975 some of the historic features of Huế were neglected, because the victorious communist regime and some other Vietnamese saw them as relics of the feudal regime. Liberalising reforms ended these policies, and some historic areas and buildings are being restored.
sections.legacy:
The legacy of the Nguyễn capital is a complex of imperial palaces, tombs and temples that UNESCO has designated. Alongside its moat and stone walls, the complex includes the Imperial City with its palaces and shrines, the Forbidden Purple City, a replica of the Royal Theatre, and temples and monuments in the outskirts. Along the Perfume River lie the tombs of several emperors, among them Minh Mạng, Khải Định and Tự Đức. The Thiên Mụ Temple is the largest pagoda in Huế and the official symbol of the city, and outside the city stands the religious site known as Nam Giao Hill, or Heaven's Altar.

Restoration of the historic areas has continued: the Kien Trung Palace was fully reconstructed in 2024. The city is also a centre of learning and medicine, with Huế University, whose colleges include medicine and pharmacy, arts, sciences, forestry and agriculture, economics and music. The Huế Central Hospital, founded in 1894, is managed by the Ministry of Health.

In 2025 Huế became Vietnam's sixth centrally governed municipality. The National Assembly passed a resolution that merged the city with the rest of Thừa Thiên Huế province, and the former provincial city was divided into two districts, Phú Xuân and Thuận Hóa.

summary: Huế, on the Perfume River in central Vietnam, grew from the Thuận Hóa region that Champa ceded to Đại Việt in 1306. As Phú Xuân it was the seat of the Nguyễn lords, and from 1802 to 1945 it was the capital of Vietnam under the Nguyễn dynasty. In 1968 it was the scene of one of the longest battles of the Vietnam War.
notes: SOURCES: only wp/hue.txt exists (no history article). The article contains nothing about the Battle of Huế of 1968 or the killings of that year: its only wartime facts are that the Forbidden Purple City 'was damaged during the Vietnam War' and the Thích Quảng Đức protest of 1963. I could not tell the battle or the killings from the article, and left them out; the editor must supply them from another source if wanted. The crises section is therefore short on violence and padded with the dynastic wars, post-1975 neglect and the 1999 floods.

GARBLED: the article says 'Thuận Hóa and Phú Xuân became the location of the Đại Việt kingdom once Nguyễn Hoàng was appointed head of Thuận Hóa (1511–1558)', which conflicts with Hoàng's later 1558–1613 dates and with the 1592 passage; left out. I used 1558 to 1613 for Hoàng's lordship as the article does.
START: no founding date; I used the 4th century CE (Lâm Ấp ruins, the oldest ruins) as c. 300 with circa true. The city as such (Phú Xuân) dates from 1687 in the article.

The article says the lords 'moved palaces to Kim Long (1636), where they would eventually base their operations in Phú Xuân (1687)', and that Phú Xuân 'became the provincial capital in 1687'; I used both as given.
The Trịnh capture is given as 1775 in both the lead and the History; the lead also says Đàng Trong's capital 1738 to 1775.

The article gives Kandarpapura's location as Long Tho Hill 'three kilometers to the west of the city' and says the ruins date back to the 4th century CE only for the Lâm Ấp kingdom; the link between that kingdom and Kandarpapura is hedged by the article itself, and I kept the hedge.

The wording on cuisine ('a vestige of its royal cuisine') is attributed to the article in the text ('which the article calls'); the editor may prefer to cut that phrase. The sentence about Thiên Mụ as 'official symbol' and the UNESCO designation are as the article states them.

Left out: tourism figures, the economy and brewery, airport, twin towns, climate figures, biodiversity, population figures (the only figure is for the province in 2015) and the administrative division.

'Nguyễn Ánh rebuilt the citadel entirely' is as the article states; the dates of individual buildings (the Flag Tower, tombs) are not given beyond 'a legacy from its time as a capital of the Nguyễn dynasty'.

REVISION (1968): crises section rewritten. Removed the first paragraph (the Nguyễn–Trịnh–Tây Sơn wars, already in 'rulers'), the sentence that the Forbidden Purple City was damaged in the Vietnam War (now covered by the battle paragraph), the Communist Party's 'feudal and reactionary' sentence, and the 1999 floods paragraph, to fit 1,900 characters. Event for 1775 dropped to keep 8 events; 1968 event added; summary gains one sentence. Sources: wp2/hue-battle.txt and wp2/hue-massacre.txt.

DISAGREEMENTS: the massacre article says the battle lasted 26 days, the battle article 31 January to 2 March (I used the dates). The massacre article gives 2,800 to 6,000 dead and 5-10% of the population; the battle article gives 300 to 6,000 for executions and 'almost 6,000' as the upper estimate of civilians killed by PAVN-VC; I gave 2,800 to almost 6,000 as the battle article's range for killings, and Pike's 2,800. The battle article says the city was 'virtually destroyed' and 80% destroyed; the Citadel's own damage is not quantified. Fallaci's claim of up to 8,000 deaths including American bombing, and Karnow's report of South Vietnamese teams' graves, were left out. The battle article's lead says civilian dead of 5,800 to 8,000 'including more than 2,000 executed'; Willbanks and Bowden are named as in its casualty section.
